title: Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act
summary: The bill amends Section 104(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code so that damages received on account of a sexual act or sexual contact — as defined in 18 U.S.C. 2246 — are excluded from gross income alongside the existing exclusion for personal physical injury or physical sickness. It also adds a new Section 104(d) that treats such damages as substantiated when the judgment or agreement states they are on account of a sexual act or contact, and bars the IRS from denying substantiation solely for lack of medical records. Punitive damages remain taxable. The amendments apply to judgments and agreements made after enactment.
brief: Adds a Section 104(a)(2) exclusion for sexual-assault damages, with a substantiation rule that credits the judgment/agreement's own characterization and bars a medical-records-only denial.

top_lines.headline: New Tax Exemption
subs: Sexual assault and abuse damages excluded from gross income — no visible injury or medical records required
Applies to non-punitive damages from judgments and settlements entered after enactment

top_lines.headline: Burden of Proof Shift
subs: IRS must prove damages are not on account of sexual acts if the judgment or agreement says they are
Medical records alone cannot be required to deny the exemption

likelihoodReason: The bill addresses a sympathetic population with bipartisan appeal — sexual assault survivors facing unexpected tax liability — and passed the House. However, only 3 cosponsors and no Senate companion bill has been identified. Tax exclusions for personal injury damages have historically attracted broad support, making Senate passage plausible but not certain without floor time being scheduled.

items.main: Names the Act the “Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act.”
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Amends Section 104(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to exclude from gross income damages received on account of any sexual act (as defined in 18 U.S.C. 2246(2)) or sexual contact (as defined in 18 U.S.C. 2246(3)), other than punitive damages.
items.detail: The prior text of Section 104(a)(2) — "on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness" — is struck and replaced with a two-branch structure: subparagraph (A) preserves personal physical injuries or physical sickness, and subparagraph (B) adds any sexual act or sexual contact as defined in 18 U.S.C. 2246(2)-(3). Punitive damages remain outside the exclusion. The amendments apply to amounts received pursuant to judgments made, and agreements entered into, after the date of enactment.

items.main: New Section 104(d) establishes that damages are substantiated as on account of sexual act or contact if the judgment or agreement so states, and prohibits denying the exclusion solely for lack of medical records.
items.detail: Damages shall be treated as on account of a sexual act or contact if the judgment or agreement providing for them states so, and shall not be treated as inadequately substantiated merely because there are no medical records of the act or contact. A judgment is treated as made after enactment if the first payment pursuant to it is received after enactment. An agreement that replaces, supersedes, or revises an agreement entered into before enactment does not qualify as a new post-enactment agreement.

items.main: Requires the Secretary of the Treasury to conduct a public awareness program about the new exclusion in consultation with the Department of Justice Office on Violence Against Women.
items.detail: The Secretary must work with the Department of Justice Office on Violence Against Women and other relevant federal agencies to promote public awareness of the exclusion from gross income provided by the new Section 104(a)(2)(B). No timeline, funding level, or required outreach methods are specified in the bill.

underreported.summary: An agreement that replaces, supersedes, or revises a pre-enactment agreement does not qualify as a new post-enactment agreement, even if the replacement is reached after enactment.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose is to extend the tax exemption to sexual assault survivors. This provision specifically bars survivors who renegotiate or revise a pre-existing settlement after enactment from accessing the new exemption, a limitation not apparent from the bill's title or the headline exemption provision.

criticisms.why: Mr. Speaker, we hear all the time about the high-profile civil cases involving sexual abuse. I am thinking about the accounts of trusted gymnast physicians abusing star athletes and the victims of Jeffrey Epstein and many of his associates. We even hear about sexual assault that occurs within our own body, and we have to address that problem. Let's just take a moment to acknowledge that all sexual abuse does not make the headlines.

gaps: The bill applies to amounts received under judgments made and agreements entered after enactment but does not address the tax treatment of damages already received under pre-enactment judgments that are still paying out.
The bill requires a public awareness program but specifies no timeline, appropriated funding, or minimum required outreach activities.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smith
featured_quotes.text: Survivors of sexual assault face a long road to recovery without having to battle with the IRS over keeping the compensatory damages or settlements that they receive. Unfortunately, right now, the burden of proof that a sexual assault survivor would have to provide to the IRS, including medical records to prove that they deserve to have their settlement funds excluded from gross income for tax purposes, ignores the fact that such victims often do not have the same observable physical injuries that other victims of assault might have.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smucker
featured_quotes.text: I think the chairman and Ms. Moore both have described it really well. The core problem here, first of all, we believe our current law already says that any victim of physical abuse and any victim of sexual abuse who receives a settlement does not owe tax on that settlement, which makes complete sense.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Moore
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, we hear all the time about the high-profile civil cases involving sexual abuse. I am thinking about the accounts of trusted gymnast physicians abusing star athletes and the victims of Jeffrey Epstein and many of his associates. We even hear about sexual assault that occurs within our own body, and we have to address that problem. Let's just take a moment to acknowledge that all sexual abuse does not make the headlines.

added: Section 104(a)(2)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 — tax exclusion for non-punitive damages on account of sexual acts or sexual contact, with no physical injury or medical records requirement
Section 104(d) — burden of proof rule placing the obligation on the IRS to disprove the characterization in any judgment or agreement stating damages are on account of sexual acts or contact
Requirement for the Secretary of the Treasury to conduct a public awareness program in consultation with the Department of Justice Office on Violence Against Women
Exclusion now applies "whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries of such act or contact" — added directly into new subparagraph (B)
New subsection (d): a no-inference rule barring any inference about whether "personal physical injuries or physical sickness" requires medical records or observable injuries
modified: Substantiation provision replaced with a burden-of-proof rule: a stating decision/agreement is "credible evidence" under section 7491(a) and the taxpayer is treated as meeting section 7491(a)(2) (was a limitation barring denial "merely because there are no medical records")
"Judgment" terminology changed to "decision" throughout the effective-date rules
removed: Removed the standalone "Prohibition on medical records requirement" paragraph (its substance folded into subparagraph (B) and the new burden-of-proof subsection)
